title_en: Jim Dahle: Is Avoiding Taxes Costing You Money?
title_zh: Jim Dahle：过度避税，反而在让你亏钱吗？
subtitle_zh: White Coat Investor 创始人 Jim Dahle 谈避税、私募投资与'足够好'的投资哲学。
summary_zh: 本期 The Long View 由 Christine Benz 与 Amy Arnott 对话急诊科医生、White Coat Investor 创始人 Dr. Jim Dahle，核心议题是：对高收入专业人士而言，过度执着于避税，反而可能拖累长期回报。Dahle 主张"税务意识"（tax-aware）而非"税务驱动"（tax-driven）的投资框架——节税应服务于资产配置与复利目标，而不是本末倒置。他复盘了自己从一味"优化每一分钱"到成为"康复中的优化者"（recovering optimizer）的转变：与其在税务细枝末节上耗费心力，不如把储蓄率、资产配置与行为纪律这些真正决定财富的大变量做对。节目也谈到面向医生等高薪人群的高费率、高佣金产品陷阱，如何用低成本指数基金、backdoor Roth、税务亏损收割（tax-loss harvesting）等工具理性节税，以及"足够好"（good enough）的投资哲学。Dahle 还分享了行医经历如何塑造他对风险与"够用"的理解，并解释为何把部分遗产提前转移给子女、设立"20多岁基金"，让下一代在人生早期就拥有财务试错的空间。整体是一堂给高收入专业人士的"别为省税而亏钱"的实用课。

turns.en: When you take more interest rate risk, the yield is higher and the best predictor of your long term returns is the current yield. turns.en: I have tried both. And what I have discovered is it was a little more of a hassle than I was willing to deal with to build out a long tips ladder. And I think it's a very great strategy. It's wonderful strategy for somebody who's retiring with just enough, meaning, you know, they want to spend approximately 4% ish of their portfolio.
turns.zh: 两种我都试过。我发现的是，搭建一个长长的 TIPS 阶梯，比我愿意应付的麻烦要多。我觉得这是个非常好的策略。对于那些'刚好够用'退休的人来说是个很棒的策略，也就是说，他们想花掉大约 4% 左右的组合。

turns.en: And thankfully we've been lucky enough or blessed enough or whatever you want to call out that we're probably going to be spending significantly less than that. And so this sequence of returns risk strategy that we're going to be using is mostly just not spending that much of our portfolio.
turns.zh: 而幸运的是，我们足够幸运——或者说足够有福气，随你怎么说——我们大概会花得远少于此。所以我们要用的这个应对收益顺序风险的策略，基本上就是别从组合里花太多。

turns.en: And so we don't necessarily need a great other sequence of returns risk solution like a tips ladder. And the truth is when you're building a tips ladder, what you really have is you've built a fund, right? When you look at your 20 or 30 individual tips each maturing in a different year, you
turns.zh: 所以我们不一定需要一个像 TIPS 阶梯那样出色的收益顺序风险解决方案。而事实是，当你搭建一个 TIPS 阶梯时，你其实是在造一只基金，对吧？当你看着你那 20 只、30 只各自在不同年份到期的单只 TIPS 时，你

turns.en: know, that really doesn't perform all that differently from a fund with the same duration as your overall portfolio. And although it'll cost you a little bit to buy a fund, maybe it's five or 10 basis points from a good bond fund, it's worth the convenience for us.
turns.zh: 知道，它的表现跟一只久期（duration）和你整体组合相同的基金其实差不了太多。虽然买一只基金会花你一点成本，也许是一只优质债券基金的五个或十个基点，但对我们来说这份便利值得。

turns.en: And so we've decided just to use a single tips ETF and we're slowly liquidating that bond ladder that we had started constructing just because it was too much of a pain. I turned to Katie, my wife, and said, do you want to deal with this or something that happens to me? And she said, no, let's just put it in a bond fund.
turns.zh: 所以我们决定就用一只 TIPS ETF，并且正在慢慢清掉我们当初开始搭建的那个债券阶梯，就因为它太麻烦了。我转向我的妻子 Katie，说，万一我出点什么事，你想接手处理这个吗？她说，不想，我们就放进一只债券基金吧。

turns.en: We have enough money. And that's what we're doing. And so I think you can make a good case either way. I think it's more important if sequence of returns risk is more significant in your life to be thinking about these things, to be thinking about building a tips ladder, to be thinking
turns.zh: 我们有足够的钱。这就是我们在做的。所以我觉得两种方式都能讲得通。如果收益顺序风险在你人生中更重大，那么更重要的是去思考这些事情：去考虑搭建 TIPS 阶梯，去考虑

turns.en: about using a single premium immediate annuity or two or three, to be thinking about delaying social security until 70, to be thinking about these things that people do to put a floor under the retirement spending to make sure they don't run out of money to protect against sequence of returns risk.
turns.zh: 使用一份、两份或三份单期缴即时年金（single premium immediate annuity），去考虑把社会保障金（Social Security）推迟到 70 岁再领，去思考人们为退休支出设置一个下限、确保不会把钱花光、防范收益顺序风险而做的那些事。

turns.en: So with the growth in wealth for individual investors and more people owning portfolios with seven or even more digits, we've also seen a big push for more complicated investment approaches, including private equity and private credit. What are your thoughts on that?
turns.zh: 随着个人投资者财富的增长、越来越多的人拥有七位数甚至更多的组合，我们也看到有人在大力推动更复杂的投资方式，包括私募股权（private equity）和私募信贷（private credit）。你怎么看？

turns.en: You know, it's interesting to see that push when US large cap stocks have done so well in the last few years. And you would think people would be going, oh, I just want to load up on my S&P 500 index fund because it's crushing it and it's super easy.
turns.zh: 你知道，有意思的是，在美国大盘股过去几年表现如此出色的时候，还有这种推动。你会以为人们会想，哦，我只想加仓我的标普 500 指数基金，因为它太猛了，而且超级简单。

turns.en: It is dramatically easier to invest in a portfolio of index funds or even a target retirement fund than to step into the private investing market. I had the opportunity to stand on the New York Stock Exchange this last week. And it's pretty fun to visit the mecca of capitalism in that way, but we don't realize
turns.zh: 投资一篮子指数基金、甚至一只目标退休基金（target retirement fund），比踏入私募投资市场要容易太多了。上周我有机会站在纽约证券交易所（New York Stock Exchange）里。以那种方式造访资本主义的圣地还挺好玩的，但我们没意识到，

turns.en: what a wonderful blessing it is for us to be able to have the transparency and the rules based market that we do to be able to invest. And obviously that's only present for publicly traded investments. Once you step into the private world, all of that is gone.
turns.zh: 能够拥有我们所拥有的这种透明度和基于规则的市场来进行投资，是多么美好的一种恩赐。而显然，这只存在于公开交易的投资中。一旦你踏入私募世界，所有这些都没了。

turns.en: Your protections from the SEC and FINRA are dramatically less in the private world. And that's why most of these investments require you to be either an accredited investor, which is generally somebody with a million dollars in investments or more, or even a qualified
turns.zh: 在私募世界里，你从 SEC 和 FINRA 那里获得的保护要少得多。这就是为什么这类投资大多要求你要么是合格投资者（accredited investor）——通常指拥有 100 万美元及以上投资资产的人——要么是合格

turns.en: purchaser, which is someone with at least five million in investments or more, because you're not as protected. You know, these investments can and do go to zero. They're often highly leveraged. And while not, you know, most people running private investments are not scammers, but it's
turns.zh: 购买者（qualified purchaser），也就是拥有至少 500 万美元投资资产的人，因为你受到的保护更少。你知道，这类投资可能、而且确实会归零。它们往往高度杠杆化。虽然——你知道，运作私募投资的大多数人不是骗子，但

turns.en: far easier for a scammer to hide out in private investments than it is in publicly traded investments. So there are lots of reasons not to enter the private investing market at all. That said, there are also some reasons that it might be worthwhile for some people. For example, these investments tend to be more illiquid.
turns.zh: 骗子躲在私募投资里，比躲在公开交易投资里要容易得多。所以有很多理由让你根本别进入私募投资市场。话虽如此，也有一些理由说明它对某些人可能是值得的。比如，这类投资往往流动性更差。

turns.en: And you think, well, that's a bad thing, not a good thing. But if you can be paid for taking some illiquidity with some portion of your portfolio, well, a lot of us are interested in that, right? If you can get an extra one or two or three percent return because you're willing to have
turns.zh: 你会想，嗯，那是坏事，不是好事。但如果你能因为承受一部分组合的流动性差而获得报酬，那么我们很多人对此是有兴趣的，对吧？如果你能因为愿意把钱锁定

turns.en: your money tied up for a year or three, well, I'm willing to do that with some portion of my portfolio in order to earn more. That sounds like a good trade off to me. And I think a lot of people look at it that way as well. A lot of people also hate market volatility.
turns.zh: 一年或三年而多拿一、两、三个百分点的回报，那么我愿意拿组合的一部分这么做，以赚取更多。这在我看来是笔不错的取舍。我觉得很多人也是这么看的。还有很多人非常讨厌市场波动。

turns.en: And while all the volatility we've seen in the last three or four years seems to be upward, they can remember 2008. They can remember 2011 and 2018 and 2020 and 2022 and even the dot com meltdown. And I'm not sure there's a lot of investors around the store remember 87, much less the stagflation of the 70s.
turns.zh: 虽然过去三四年我们看到的所有波动似乎都是向上的，但他们记得 2008 年。他们记得 2011、2018、2020 和 2022 年，甚至记得互联网泡沫的崩盘。而我不确定还有多少投资人仍然记得 1987 年，更别说 70 年代的滞胀了。

turns.en: But markets also go down and the publicly traded markets feel so much more volatile. And maybe the private market is just hiding that volatility better because they're not marked to market each day. But they feel so much more volatile and that bothers a lot of people.
turns.zh: 但市场也会下跌，而公开交易市场感觉波动大得多。也许私募市场只是把波动藏得更好，因为它们不每天按市价计价（marked to market）。但公开市场感觉波动大得多，这让很多人不安。

turns.en: And when you own a portfolio of rental properties down your street or you're invested in these private investments that aren't marked to market, your portfolio doesn't feel quite as volatile. And so people appreciate that as well. And obviously there are lots of great companies out there and great real estate investments that
turns.zh: 而当你持有一整条街上的出租房组合，或者你投资了这些不按市价计价的私募投资时，你的组合感觉就不那么剧烈波动了。所以人们也欣赏这一点。而且显然市面上有很多很棒的公司和很棒的房地产投资

turns.en: are not publicly traded. Some of the highest returning companies in America are small businesses that are still growing that are still on a hockey stick kind of trajectory that are growing or 20 and 30 and 40 percent per year. Well, that's a lot harder to do when your Google or Amazon or X on and you're already large.
turns.zh: 并没有公开上市。美国回报率最高的一些公司，是那些仍在成长、仍处于曲棍球杆式（hockey-stick）增长轨迹、每年以 20%、30%、40% 增长的小企业。嗯，当你已经是 Google、Amazon 或 Exxon 那么大时，就难多了。

turns.en: And some people get excited about being in these smaller companies and these privately traded companies that maybe don't have to answer to quite so many shareholders. And they appreciate their particular missions or they appreciate their agility in those sorts of things.
turns.zh: 有些人对能参与这些更小的公司、这些私募交易的公司感到兴奋，它们也许不必向那么多股东负责。他们欣赏这些公司独特的使命，或者欣赏它们的敏捷之类的东西。

turns.en: I mean, obviously until a few months ago, even a big company like SpaceX was not a publicly traded company. And if you wanted a piece of that prior to a going public, you had to be willing to invest in private investments. And so I get the appeal, I think for a lot of people, their investments that are sold
turns.zh: 我是说，显然就在几个月前，连 SpaceX 这样的大公司都还不是上市公司。如果你想在它上市之前分一杯羹，你就得愿意投资私募投资。所以我理解它的吸引力。我觉得对很多人来说，这些是被'卖'给你

turns.en: rather than bought, they're certainly optional. You do not have to invest in private investments to become financially independent and have a wonderful retirement. But I think if you are eligible for them and not afraid to have a bit more of a complex illiquid portfolio, you may find something in there that makes sense for you.
turns.zh: 而不是你主动'买'的投资，它们当然是可选的。你不必投资私募投资就能实现财务独立、拥有美好的退休生活。但我觉得，如果你符合条件，又不害怕持有一个更复杂、流动性更差的组合，你也许能在里面找到对你有意义的东西。

turns.en: Was reading through your conversation with Larry Swedro where you talked about private credit? You felt that you were a little warmer to private credit than private equity. Wondering if you can walk us through your thinking there. And also what role you would see private credit playing in a portfolio?
turns.zh: 我读了你和 Larry Swedroe 的那场对话，你在里面谈到了私募信贷。你觉得你对私募信贷比对私募股权要更热络一些。想请你带我们理清一下你在这方面的思路。以及你会看到私募信贷在组合中扮演什么角色？

turns.en: You talked about how bonds are the low risk portion of your portfolio. So presumably you wouldn't want to hold private credit as a surrogate for high quality fixed income. But maybe just talk us through your thinking there. Sure. Well, a lot of people, particularly when they step into the private markets, they
turns.zh: 你谈到债券是你组合中低风险的那部分。所以想必你不会想把私募信贷当作高质量固定收益的替代品来持有。不过还是请你给我们讲讲你的思路吧。好的。嗯，很多人，尤其是在踏入私募市场时，他们

turns.en: get this mindset of, I got to shoot the lights out. I got to hit a home run here, you know, if I'm not going to be buying index funds or I'm not going to be buying, you know, a tips ladder, I might as well go for the fences. And that is not the case. You don't have to do that even in the private markets.
turns.zh: 会有这种心态：我得全力一搏，我得在这里打出本垒打。你知道，既然我不打算买指数基金、也不打算买 TIPS 阶梯，那我干脆放手一搏。但事实并非如此。即使在私募市场里，你也不必那样做。

turns.en: There are ways to invest with less risk. And I think this is perhaps best illustrated in the real estate markets, right? You can be the equity investor in the real estate capital stack. And you have the highest potential returns. If the investment ends up doing really well, you get to keep all the extra.
turns.zh: 有一些风险更低的投资方式。我觉得这一点也许在房地产市场里体现得最好，对吧？你可以做房地产资本结构（capital stack）里的股权投资者。你拥有最高的潜在回报。如果这笔投资最终做得非常好，多出来的部分都归你。

turns.en: And then there's mezzanine debt and preferred equity, these kind of intermediate positions. And then there's the lender, the lender in first position. And that is the person taking the least amount of risk in the investment. So often when I talk to people who want to get into real estate investing, I mentioned
turns.zh: 然后是夹层债务（mezzanine debt）和优先股权（preferred equity），这些是中间位置。再然后是第一顺位的贷款人。那才是这笔投资中承担风险最小的人。所以当我跟想进入房地产投资的人聊时，我常常

turns.en: to them that you don't have to take maximum risk, especially with your first few investments. You can invest on the debt side. You can be the lender in essence. And yes, you're not going to get 25% returns if it does really well. You're only going to get whatever, eight or nine percent returns if it does really well. And that's okay.
turns.zh: 跟他们说，你不必承担最大风险，尤其是你的头几笔投资。你可以投在债务那一边。你本质上可以做那个贷款人。是的，如果它做得非常好，你不会拿到 25% 的回报，你只会拿到比如 8% 或 9% 的回报。那没关系。

turns.en: You got to be okay with that. But you're taking dramatically less risk. I have had a real estate investment. And in this case, unfortunately, I was the equity investor. And when rates went up in 2022, that was really bad for leverage real estate investments.
turns.zh: 你得能接受这一点。但你承担的风险要小得多。我曾有一笔房地产投资。在这个案例里，很遗憾，我是股权投资者。当 2022 年利率上升时，那对杠杆化的房地产投资非常不利。

turns.en: And so with this particular investment, all the equity investors were cleaned out. They had 100% loss of their investment. But the mezzanine debt, the preferred equity, they got all their cash back as well as their interest. And of course, the primary lender, the debt investor got all their money back and all the interest they were due.
turns.zh: 所以在这笔特定的投资里，所有股权投资者都被清空了。他们的投资 100% 亏损。但夹层债务、优先股权，他们拿回了全部本金以及利息。当然，主要贷款人、也就是债务投资者，拿回了全部本金和他们应得的所有利息。

turns.en: So the only people who lost money were the equity investors. And so that is the appeal of being a debt investor is you're taking less risk. You're in a better position in the capital stack. So that can be really appealing to people. One of the downsides of being that debt investor, of course, is that it's not a very tax-efficient
turns.zh: 所以唯一亏钱的只有股权投资者。这就是做债务投资者的吸引力所在——你承担更小的风险，你在资本结构里的位置更好。所以这对很多人可能非常有吸引力。当然，做债务投资者的一个缺点，是它不是很有税收效率

turns.en: investment, right? Pretty much your entire return is being paid out to you every year and you're paying taxes on an ordinary income tax rates. And so people prefer to have these sorts of investments inside some type of a tax protected vehicle, whether that's a retirement account or an annuity or some sort of private
turns.zh: 的投资，对吧？基本上你全部的回报每年都支付给你，你要按普通收入税率交税。所以人们更愿意把这类投资放在某种税收保护的载体里，无论是退休账户、年金，还是某种私募

turns.en: placement, life insurance or something where it's not being completely taxed every year. That's the real downside to investing on the debt portion of the portfolio. It's just really tax inefficient. And if you're already in a high tax bracket, that can eat up a pretty significant portion of your return.
turns.zh: 人寿保险，或者某种不会被每年完全课税的东西。这就是投在组合债务部分真正的缺点，它实在是很没有税收效率。而如果你已经处在高税率区间，那可能吃掉你回报里相当大的一部分。

turns.en: So if someone does want to venture into private credit in a more tax-efficient way, what type of expenses would they be looking at? Well, I mean, I think to do it in a tax-efficient way, you need to do it inside something like a retirement account, like a self-directed IRA or a self-directed solo 401k or something like that.
turns.zh: 那么如果有人确实想以更有税收效率的方式涉足私募信贷，他们会面对什么样的费用？嗯，我的意思是，我觉得要以税收高效的方式做，你需要把它放在某种退休账户里，比如自主管理 IRA（self-directed IRA）或个人 solo 401(k)，之类的东西。

turns.en: But the expenses on these investments are highly variable, right? I mean, investing in this, great thanks for this, belongs to Jack Bogle. I mean, particularly in the public markets, is essentially free now, right? If you want to go by all the stocks in the world, you're going to be paying less than ten basis points on that index fund.
turns.zh: 但这类投资的费用差异非常大，对吧？我是说，投资这件事——这份功劳要归于 Jack Bogle——尤其在公开市场里，如今基本上是免费的，对吧？如果你想买下全世界的股票，你为那只指数基金支付的费用还不到十个基点。

turns.en: In fact, Fidelity's got a few that they don't even charge an expense ratio at zero. No, I don't think that's significantly different from paying three basis points to Vanguard. But it's free. Essentially, it's investing is free now in the publicly traded markets. And that's not the case in the private markets.
turns.zh: 事实上，Fidelity 有几只基金连费用比率都不收，是零。不，我觉得这跟向 Vanguard 付三个基点没什么实质性区别。但它是免费的。基本上，在公开交易市场里，投资如今是免费的。而在私募市场里则不是这样。

turns.en: So it wouldn't be unusual at all for you to be paying on something like a private real estate debt fund. It wouldn't be unusual at all for you to be paying a fee of 1% of the assets plus 20% of the return above something like 8% a year. That would be pretty typical fee structure for these sorts of investments.
turns.zh: 所以，在类似私募房地产债务基金这样的东西上，你要付的费用一点也不奇怪。你付出 1% 的资产费用，再加上超过某个门槛（比如年化 8%）部分回报的 20%，这一点也不奇怪。那会是这类投资相当典型的费用结构。

turns.en: So you have to look at and go, yes, that after fee return is still worth it to me to be able to invest in this asset class. And the way I look at it is this isn't a bond replacement. This isn't a stock replacement. It's something else. It's another asset class. It acts completely different from those two.
turns.zh: 所以你得看着它，然后想，是的，即便扣完费，这个回报对我投资这个资产类别来说仍然值得。而我看它的方式是：这不是债券的替代品，也不是股票的替代品，它是别的东西，是另一个资产类别。它的表现和那两者完全不同。

turns.en: Equity real estate is different from debt real estate and debt real estate is different from bonds. And so if you're going to have an allocation to these sorts of things, it's separate from your stock allocation, it's separate from your bond allocation. So sticking with complicated strategies that wealthy investors are embracing, one that
turns.zh: 股权型房地产不同于债务型房地产，而债务型房地产又不同于债券。所以如果你要配置这类东西，它独立于你的股票配置，也独立于你的债券配置。那么继续谈有钱投资者正在拥抱的复杂策略，其中一个

turns.en: has been getting the heavy sell over the past few years is this idea of direct indexing or other strategies that use active tax loss harvesting. Can you talk about that? You have been, I think, pretty critical of those strategies because they introduce so much additional complexity. But maybe talk about your thinking.
turns.zh: 过去几年被大力推销的，就是直接指数化（direct indexing）这个概念，或者其他使用主动税损收割（tax-loss harvesting）的策略。你能谈谈这个吗？我记得你对这些策略一直挺批评的，因为它们引入了太多额外的复杂性。不过还是说说你的想法吧。

turns.en: Yeah, I don't know that I say I'm critical about it. I think some of these companies are overselling the value of the losses. And let me explain. I'm a fan of tax loss harvesting. I tax loss harvest art taxable account when there's a loss. I see no reason to hold on to it.
turns.zh: 是啊，我不确定我会说我批评它。我觉得其中一些公司在夸大这些亏损的价值。让我解释一下。我是税损收割的拥护者。只要我的应税账户里出现亏损，我就做税损收割。我看不出有什么理由死抱着它不放。

turns.en: So I sell that investment by something similar to it, but not in the words of the IRS substantially identical and basically book that loss without really changing my asset allocation. And so I've been doing this for years, you know, in 2020 and 2022, we're opportunities to harvest large losses.
turns.zh: 所以我会卖掉那笔投资，买入一只类似、但用 IRS 的话说并非'实质相同'（substantially identical）的标的，基本上就把那笔亏损入账，而并没有真正改变我的资产配置。我这么做已经很多年了，你知道，2020 年和 2022 年都是收割大额亏损的机会。

turns.en: And so we're carrying around seven figures of losses. But on your taxes each year, you can only use $3,000 of those losses against your ordinary income. It doesn't do you any good to have $300,000 of them if that's the only way you're using these losses. And so you've got to have some other reason to have the losses.
turns.zh: 所以我们手里攒着七位数的亏损。但每年报税时，你只能用其中的 3,000 美元来抵扣你的普通收入。如果这是你使用这些亏损的唯一方式，那么手里有 30 万美元的亏损对你没有任何好处。所以你得有别的原因来持有这些亏损。

turns.en: And it might be selling some of the winners in your portfolio to generate retirement income. You could use some losses for that for sure. But you know, if you're really trying to get more losses than a few tens of thousands, you've got to have something in your future that seems to suggest you can benefit from those.
turns.zh: 那可能是卖出你组合里的一些盈利头寸来产生退休收入。你当然可以用一些亏损来对冲那部分。但你知道，如果你真想获得比几万美元更多的亏损，你的未来得有某些东西表明你能从中受益。

turns.en: Whether that's the sale of a business or a medical or dental practice or whether that's selling your home that's above the exempted amount, but you got to have a reason to have these losses. Otherwise, spending a bunch of money and a bunch of hassle to get the losses really isn't worthwhile. They all go away when you die.
turns.zh: 无论是出售一家企业、一家医疗或牙科诊所，还是出售你超出免税额度的房子，你总得有个理由来持有这些亏损。否则，为获取亏损而花一大堆钱、惹一堆麻烦，真的不值得。你去世时它们全都消失了。

turns.en: It's not like you get a pass them on to your errors or something. And so you got to ask yourself, how valuable would more losses be to me? And if the answer is very valuable, well, maybe now it's worth paying a little extra and dealing with a little more hassle to engage with a very low cost direct indexing provider.
turns.zh: 又不是说你能把它们传给你的继承人（heirs）之类的。所以你得问自己，更多的亏损对我有多大价值？如果答案是'非常有价值'，那么也许多付一点钱、多应付一点麻烦，去选择一家成本非常低的直接指数化服务商，就是值得的。

turns.en: But this is a little bit of a lifelong commitment to direct indexing. You really ought to plan to stick with them the rest of your life because getting out of that can eat up, you know, most of all the losses that you booked along the way in order to cancel out the gains to move back into, you know, say an index fund portfolio.
turns.zh: 但这有点像是与直接指数化订下了一份终身承诺。你真的应该打算余生都跟着他们，因为从中退出可能会吃掉你一路上入账的大部分亏损——那些为了抵消收益、以便重新回到比如指数基金组合而记账的亏损。

turns.en: And so if you leave this direct indexing provider and they were direct indexing the S&P 500 for you, they're going to hand you 500 stocks. You're going to have 500 individual stock positions. And you'll have to go through the hassle of selling each of those and deciding which
turns.zh: 所以如果你离开这家直接指数化服务商，而他们一直在为你直接指数化标普 500，他们会把 500 只股票交还给你。你将持有 500 个单独的股票头寸。你不得不经历卖掉每一只、并判断哪

turns.en: ones have, you know, substantial capital gains, which ones don't maybe holding onto the ones that do and building your portfolio around that. It's not an insignificant amount of hassle. So don't go down that route if the losses don't have significant value to you in the first place.
turns.zh: 些有可观资本利得、哪些没有的麻烦，也许会保留那些有利得的、围绕它们来重建你的组合。这不是一个小麻烦。所以如果这些亏损一开始对你就没有重大价值，那就别走这条路。

turns.en: But if you're looking at selling a $5 million business down the road and you could sure use another million or $2 million in losses to put against those capital gains, it may be worthwhile for you to look into some of these strategies to get more capital losses.
turns.zh: 但如果你打算日后卖掉一家 500 万美元的企业，而你正好需要再多一百万或两百万美元的亏损来对冲那些资本利得，那么研究一下这些能获取更多资本亏损的策略，对你也许是值得的。

turns.en: We also wanted to talk a bit about your evolution as an investor and you've written that you first started getting interested in investing in personal finance when you were in the middle of your medical residency. I'm wondering how your own leanings as an investor have changed as your portfolio has grown.
turns.zh: 我们也想聊聊你作为一名投资者的演变。你写过，你最早是在住院医师培训进行到一半时，开始对投资和个人理财产生兴趣的。我想知道，随着你的组合增长，你自己作为投资者的倾向发生了怎样的变化。

turns.en: It seems like you're very comfortable with kind of good enough investing and avoiding complexity. Were you always that way or have you evolved more in that direction over time? As a financial advisor, you've got your clients back and we've got yours. With Vanguard's actually managed bond funds, you're backed by consistent performance with
turns.zh: 看起来你对那种'足够好'的投资、对避开复杂性非常自如。你一直都这样吗，还是随着时间推移越来越往这个方向演变？作为一名财务顾问，你守护着客户，而我们守护着你。借助 Vanguard 的主动管理型债券基金，你有稳健表现的支撑，

turns.en: a low cost edge for an advantage that keeps compounding and compounding and compounding. Sorry, quick break for legal, to learn more visit Vanguard.com slash audio, all investing is subject to risk investments and bonds are subject to interest rate credit and inflation
turns.zh: 还有低成本带来的优势，让这份优势不断复利、复利、再复利。抱歉，插播一段合规声明。想了解更多请访问 Vanguard.com/audio。所有投资都存在风险，投资和债券都面临利率、信用和通胀

turns.en: risk Vanguard marketing corporation distributor and compounding and compounding and compounding. Are you backed by institutional quality bond funds Vanguard? I think what happens to most people, the longer they do this and as they build wealth in particular is they move, you know, even people that are very interested in this stuff,
turns.zh: 风险。Vanguard Marketing Corporation 为分销商。复利、复利、再复利——有机构级品质的债券基金为你撑腰吗？Vanguard？我觉得，对大多数人来说，做得越久、尤其是随着财富积累，他们会转变，你知道，即使是那些对这东西非常感兴趣的人，

turns.en: they're hobbyists for lack of a better term. They move from being what we call an optimizer to a satisfacer and an optimizer is trying to eke every little bit of cash out of their budget so they can invest it for their future. They're trying to eke every little bit of extra return or every little tax advantage they
turns.zh: 暂且说是'爱好者'（hobbyists）吧。他们会从我们所说的'优化者'（optimizer）转变成'满足者'（satisficer）。优化者会想尽办法从预算里抠出每一点点现金，好为未来投资。他们会想尽办法抠出每一点点额外回报、或每一点点税收优惠，

turns.en: can get and they end up with fairly complex financial lies, fairly complex portfolios. They end up spending a lot of time for maybe pretty minor gains and after a while gains that aren't even going to change their lives at all and so I don't claim to be a completely reformed optimizer yet but I'm certainly trending in that direction.
turns.zh: 能拿的都拿，最后他们的财务生活相当复杂、组合也相当复杂。他们花了很多时间，换来的也许只是相当微小的收益，而且过一阵子，那些收益甚至根本不会改变他们的生活。所以我并不声称自己已经是一个彻底改过自新的优化者，但我确实在往那个方向走。

turns.en: I see the wisdom behind being more of a satisfacer and I'm certainly trying to do that more and more as I go. For example, we had a change in our portfolio eight or ten years ago where we just dropped three asset classes basically, we just said what are we doing?
turns.zh: 我看到了更多做一个'满足者'背后的智慧，我当然也在努力越来越多地这么做。举个例子，大约八到十年前，我们对组合做了一次调整，基本上直接砍掉了三个资产类别，我们就是在想，我们到底在干嘛？

turns.en: We need a simpler portfolio, it's too hard to manage this across five or six or seven retirement accounts. This doesn't make sense for us to be doing and we simplify our asset allocation significantly and I also just let the small things go a whole lot more than I used to and we're certainly
turns.zh: 我们需要一个更简单的组合，要在五六个甚至七个退休账户之间管理这些，太难了。这么做对我们没意义，于是我们大幅简化了资产配置，我也开始比以前更多地放过那些小事，我们当然

turns.en: much more free with our spending than we used to but I think that's pretty natural for most people as they build wealth. If you continue to be a hyper optimizer, you know, once you have enough and even beyond enough, you got to ask yourself, what am I missing out on really in my life?
turns.zh: 在花钱上比以前大方多了，但我觉得对大多数人在积累财富的过程中，这是很自然的。如果你已经拥有足够、甚至远超足够的财富，却还继续做一个超级优化者，你就得问自己：我的人生到底错过了什么？

turns.en: By virtue of doing this, is this really my favorite hobby, would I really rather be doing this and spending more time with my kids or my grandkids or whatever? And for most people, the answer is going to be no, I don't like it that much. There are other things I would rather do with my life than play with my spreadsheets.
turns.zh: 这么做，真的是我最爱的爱好吗？我真的宁愿做这个，也不愿多花时间陪我的孩子或孙辈之类的吗？对大多数人来说，答案会是'不，我没那么喜欢它。比起摆弄我的电子表格，我人生中有别的事更愿意做'。

turns.en: What I wanted to ask Jim, what were the three asset classes that went on the cutting room floor? Well, there are mostly things like large value, right? I already had money in small value and it was like, well, why do I have money in large value and small value, just to have small value in a total stock market fund?
turns.zh: 我想问问 Jim，被砍掉的那三个资产类别是什么？嗯，主要是一些像大盘价值（large value）这样的东西，对吧？我已经在小盘价值（small value）里有钱了，我就想，为什么我在大盘价值和小盘价值里都有钱，只留小盘价值、再配一只全市场股票基金不就行了？

turns.en: And we also had a small allocation. So we dropped the large value, we dropped the small, we just put it on to small value and that allowed us to drop asset classes. We also had an allocation to midcaps, a separate allocation to midcaps and we dropped that. I think those were the three asset classes we dropped.
turns.zh: 我们还有一个小盘配置。所以我们砍掉了大盘价值，砍掉了小盘，就把它并到小盘价值里，这样就能砍掉一些资产类别。我们还有一个中盘配置、一个单独的中盘配置，我们也砍掉了。我觉得那就是我们砍掉的那三个资产类别。

turns.en: So can you generalize about doctors and their proclivities as investors and maybe where they land on that optimizer-satisfacer spectrum? Well, I mean, doctors like anybody else, they run the whole spectrum, right? Yeah. You've got doctors that have not paid any attention whatsoever to their finances.
turns.zh: 那么你能不能就医生这个群体、以及他们作为投资者的倾向做个概括，也许还有他们落在'优化者—满足者'这个光谱的什么位置？嗯，我是说，医生和任何人一样，横跨整个光谱，对吧？是的。有些医生对自己的财务完全没上心。

turns.en: It's actually shocking to do net worth surveys of doctors in their 60s. You will learn that about 25% of them, despite making two or three or $400,000 a year for their entire career, do not even have a million dollars of it left. They're net worth. Everything.
turns.zh: 对 60 多岁的医生做净资产调查，结果其实很令人震惊。你会发现，他们中大约 25% 的人，尽管整个职业生涯每年赚二三十万甚至四十万美元，净资产却连 100 万美元都不到。他们的净资产——所有东西——

turns.en: House, car, retirement accounts, investments, it doesn't add up to a million dollars and they might have made eight or ten million dollars during their careers. So you've got that sort of dock on one end of the spectrum and then you've got those who become kind of investing hobbyists and really pay a lot of attention to this stuff
turns.zh: 房子、车、退休账户、投资，加起来不到 100 万美元，而他们职业生涯里可能赚了八百万到一千万美元。所以光谱的一端是那种医生，另一端则是那些成为投资'爱好者'、真的非常关注这些东西、

turns.en: and really optimize things and you combine that with a three or four or $500,000 income and it's pretty amazing what you can do. And so I think you see doctors that run a huge gamut. It is a very wide range of wealth among doctors, certainly more than a lot of people would expect considering that the incomes are often not that different.
turns.zh: 真的把各种东西都优化到位的人。你把这个跟三四十万甚至五十万美元的收入结合起来，你能做到的事是相当惊人的。所以我觉得医生群体横跨极大的范围。医生之间的财富差距非常大，考虑到他们的收入往往差别没那么大，这个差距肯定超出很多人的预料。

turns.en: But I wouldn't say that they're necessarily optimizers or satisficers. I think there's like anything else there, you know, there's some of each. You also recently wrote about the value of having a too hard pile and you shared some activities and strategies that might be in it.
turns.zh: 但我不会说他们一定是优化者或满足者。我觉得和其他任何东西一样，两种都有。你最近还写了关于设立一个'太难'堆（too-hard pile）的价值，并分享了一些可能被放进其中的活动和策略。

turns.en: What are some of the key ones or key things that you put in that pile? Yeah, there are so many things you can do with your investments. So many things you can do with your finances that just add a great deal of complexity and it isn't that it's not necessarily intelligent.
turns.zh: 你会放进那个堆里的一些关键的东西是什么？是啊，关于你的投资、你的财务，你能做的事太多了，它们只会平添大量复杂性，而且不是说它一定不明智。

turns.en: It's just that it takes an awful lot of effort to understand it, implement it and maintain it. I've run into people that use options strategies, for instance. And they're like, well, all I do is I just check every morning at about 9.45 in the morning, you know, how things are going and then make a decision on what to do that day.
turns.zh: 只是理解它、实施它、维护它需要花非常多的精力。我遇到过使用期权策略的人。他们会说，嗯，我要做的就是每天早上大约 9 点 45 分看一下情况怎么样，然后决定那天该怎么做。

turns.en: Well, that's too hard for me, right? I don't need a strategy that I got to log into investing accounts every day. I'm lucky if I log into investing accounts every month. And often I go several months without logging into investing accounts. And so any strategy that requires me to do that is by far too hard for me.
turns.zh: 嗯，那对我来说太难了，对吧？我不需要一个必须每天登录投资账户的策略。我能每月登录一次投资账户就算幸运了。而且我常常好几个月都不登录投资账户。所以任何需要我那么做的策略，对我来说都实在太难了。

turns.en: And that often includes things like options. It often includes, you know, highly leveraged types of investments. As a general rule, we've decided just not to have debt in our lives at all. Now some of our investments have debt inherent to them, but we don't actually have any personal debt.
turns.zh: 那通常包括期权之类的东西，通常也包括高度杠杆化的投资。作为一条通则，我们已经决定生活里干脆完全不要负债。现在我们的一些投资本身自带债务，但我们个人其实没有任何负债。

turns.en: No mortgage, no margin loans, no consumer debt, none of that. We just got rid of that about a decade ago in our lives. We just found our lives were a lot simpler without it. And that doesn't mean that you can't come out ahead by investing on margin. You can.
turns.zh: 没有房贷，没有保证金贷款（margin loan），没有消费债，什么都没有。大约十年前我们把那些都清掉了。我们发现没有它们，生活简单多了。这并不意味着你靠保证金投资就不能占上风。你可以。

turns.en: And some very smart people have said, maybe it's optimal to have an amount of debt, something like 15 to 35% of your assets. And we just decided, ah, too hard. It's too hard for us. That tips ladder. Too hard for us. You know, it just doesn't match us.
turns.zh: 一些非常聪明的人说过，持有一定量的债务也许是最优的，大概是你资产的 15% 到 35%。而我们就是决定，啊，太难了。对我们来说太难了。那个 TIPS 阶梯，对我们来说太难了。它就是不适合我们。

turns.en: And so you got to recognize that at the end of the day, investing is a single player game. It's you against your goals. And you only need a strategy good enough to reach your goals and then you've won the game. You don't need a strategy that's harder than that.
turns.zh: 所以你得认识到，说到底，投资是一场单人游戏。是你和你的目标之间的较量。你只需要一个足够好、能帮你达成目标的策略，然后你就赢了这场游戏。你不需要一个比那更难的策略。

turns.en: And I think most people will, if they, you know, keep looking into more and more different ways to invest and more and more ways to manage your portfolio, that they will eventually hit a level where they're like, ah, it's too hard for me. I'm not going to do that. And that's okay. That's probably a good thing for most people.
turns.zh: 我觉得大多数人如果不断地去研究越来越多不同的投资方式、越来越多管理组合的方法，他们最终会碰到一个层级，然后想，啊，这对我来说太难了，我不做那个。那没关系。对大多数人来说那可能是件好事。

turns.en: Now, everyone's going to draw that line in a different place. Some people might say, it's too much for me to pick a handful of index funds. I'm going to hire a good financial planner that offers good advice at a fair price. And that's fine too, right?
turns.zh: 当然，每个人划那条线的位置都不一样。有些人可能会说，光是挑几只指数基金对我来说都太多了，我要去请一位优秀的财务规划师，他以公道的价格提供好的建议。那也没问题，对吧？

turns.en: Everybody's somewhere along that spectrum and you've just got to figure out where you are, recognize it, not try to be somewhere else on the spectrum that doesn't fit you. So earlier, you referenced this issue with people whose portfolios have grown a lot and they're getting close to retirement.
turns.zh: 每个人都处在那个光谱的某个位置，你只需弄清楚自己在哪里，认清它，别硬要待在光谱上另一个不适合你的位置。那么早些时候，你提到了这个问题：有些人的组合增长了很多，正临近退休。

turns.en: They're not spending in line with what the planning advice would tell them they could spend. What's your response to that? I hear from some people who kind of say, stop bugging me about this because I'm fine. I like what I'm spending. What's your retort? Well, it's their money they can do what they want.
turns.zh: 他们的支出却达不到规划建议告诉他们可以花的水平。你对此怎么回应？我听到有些人会说，别再拿这事儿烦我了，因为我挺好的，我对自己的支出很满意。你怎么反驳？嗯，那是他们的钱，他们想怎么花都行。

turns.en: They're absolutely right about that. So if they want to equip being bugged, that's fine. They can quit reading your columns, Christine. But there are really two big problems in personal finance. They're both behavioral problems. And as soon as you solve the first one, it's time to start working on the second one.
turns.zh: 他们说得完全没错。所以如果他们不想再被烦，那也行，他们可以不看你的专栏了，Christine。但个人理财里其实有两大难题。它们都是行为问题。而你一旦解决了第一个，就该开始着手第二个了。

turns.en: Most people never solve the first one. And most of the people who solve the first one never solve the second one. So let me describe what these are. The first one is saving enough money that you can build a nest egg large enough to live the rest of your life. Most people, they just don't save enough money.
turns.zh: 大多数人从没解决第一个。而解决了第一个的人里，大多数也从没解决第二个。让我说说这两个是什么。第一个是存下足够的钱，让你能积累起一个足以度过余生的储备金（nest egg）。大多数人就是存的钱不够。

turns.en: If you look at the statistics, something like 40% of retirees are living on nothing but social security. They either never built a nest egg or they spent it so rapidly in retirement that it's gone. This is a big problem for people. People have a hard time doing it.
turns.zh: 如果你看统计数据，大约有 40% 的退休者只靠社会保障金生活。他们要么从没积累起储备金，要么在退休后花得太快，储备金没了。这对人们来说是个大问题。人们很难做到。

turns.en: But for those who do solve this problem, as soon as you get it solved, recognize this time to start working on the second problem, which is how to spend and give that money. And it's hard for people who have this frugal mindset that optimize their portfolios,
turns.zh: 但对那些确实解决了这个问题的人来说，一旦你解决了它，就要认识到，是时候开始着手第二个问题了，那就是如何花掉和捐出这些钱。而对那些有这种节俭心态、把自己的组合、

turns.en: optimize their financial lives, learned how to budget, carved out a big chunk of it to invest it for the future, chose a reasonable plan to invest it. It's very hard for that person to flip the switch on the day of retirement and go from being a net saver to being a net spender. Most people can't do it.
turns.zh: 把自己的财务生活都优化到极致、学会了如何做预算、从中划出一大块来为未来投资、还选了一个合理方案去投资的人来说，要在退休那天拨动开关、从一个净储蓄者变成一个净支出者，非常难。大多数人做不到。

turns.en: Statistics suggest something like six out of seven retirees aren't touching their principal at all. They're basically investing as though they're immortal. That's just not the case. They're not immortal. It is a problem. It's difficult for people to do. It takes work.
turns.zh: 统计数据表明，大约七名退休者里有六名根本没动过本金。他们基本上是在当作自己不会死那样投资。但事实并非如此。他们不是不死的。这是个问题。人们很难做到。它需要下功夫。

turns.en: I view there being five money activities in life, earning, saving, investing, spending and giving. They're all about as hard as one another. Those people who turned out to be pretty good at earning and saving and investing, you may be not be that good at spending.
turns.zh: 我把人生中的金钱活动看作有五种：赚、存、投、花、捐。它们的难度都差不多。那些最后发现自己挺擅长赚钱、存钱和投资的人，也许并不那么擅长花钱。

turns.en: There's probably some stuff you can spend money on that is going to make your life happier and the lives of others happier. There are certainly some good causes that you would support that you could give to if you're willing to put in the effort and the research and think for a few minutes about how much
turns.zh: 可能有些东西，你把钱花在上面会让你的人生更快乐、也让别人的人生更快乐。当然也有一些好的事业是你愿意支持的，只要你愿意下功夫去研究、花几分钟想一想你到底能安全地捐出

turns.en: of your money you really can give away safely. It's work, yes, but it's work that's worthwhile to get good at all five of those activities. So you and your wife have four children. What kind of things have you done to impart financial responsibility to them or teach them about investing?
turns.zh: 多少钱。是的，这需要下功夫，但把这五种活动全都做好，这份功夫是值得的。那么你和你的妻子有四个孩子。你做了哪些事来向他们灌输财务责任感，或者教他们投资？

turns.en: The first thing is we're a lot more transparent than most people are. We're transparent with friends and family and the general public and obviously that extends to our children as well. Money is not a hush, hush subject in our household. It's something that's talked about all the time. As they get older, the conversation changes.
turns.zh: 第一件事是，我们比大多数人透明得多。我们对朋友、家人和公众都透明，显然这也延伸到我们的孩子身上。在我们家，钱不是一个需要避讳的话题。它是随时都在谈论的事。随着他们长大，对话也在变化。

turns.en: Obviously you can discuss more complex things with a 17-year-old than you can with a 6-year-old. We start very early. They have some funds for their college and for their 20s and those sorts of things. They own basically all the stocks in the world in those funds.
turns.zh: 显然，你能跟一个 17 岁的孩子讨论的东西，比跟一个 6 岁的孩子要多、要复杂。我们很早就开始。他们有一些用于上大学、用于他们 20 多岁时之类的资金。那些基金里，他们基本上拥有全世界所有的股票。

turns.en: When we drive down the street and we drive past McDonald's and I point out you own that. We drive past Home Depot and I point out you own that. Every time we pass a publicly traded company and in your daily drive, you pass a lot of publicly traded companies.
turns.zh: 当我们开车上街，路过 McDonald's，我会指出来：你拥有它。路过 Home Depot，我会指出来：你拥有它。每次我们经过一家上市公司——而在你每天的通勤路上，你会经过很多上市公司——

turns.en: You can point out to your children that what it means to own something, what stocks are and what bonds are and you can teach them all these things. You can teach them about debt and you'll be surprised how young they can be and learn these basics about personal finance. We try to teach them about work.
turns.zh: 你都可以向孩子指出，拥有一样东西意味着什么、股票是什么、债券是什么，你可以教他们所有这些。你可以教他们债务，你会惊讶于他们那么小就能学会这些个人理财的基础知识。我们也试着教他们关于工作。

turns.en: We encourage them to have lemonade stands. We encourage them to do allowances. We set up matches for them for various things and then as they get into their high school years, we start getting very serious about teaching them the basics of personal finance and investing. By the time my kids leave home, they know about index funds.
turns.zh: 我们鼓励他们摆柠檬水摊。我们鼓励他们领零花钱。我们为他们各种事情设置配比（match）。等他们进入高中阶段，我们就开始非常认真地教他们个人理财和投资的基础知识。等我的孩子们离家时，他们已经懂指数基金了。

turns.en: They know about buying hold philosophies. They know about the importance of critical types of insurance. They know how retirement accounts work. They go to the required and Utah is good this way where we live. It's got mandatory personal finance class in high school and in high school, the teacher
turns.zh: 他们懂买入并持有（buy-and-hold）的理念。他们懂几类关键保险的重要性。他们懂退休账户怎么运作。他们上必修课——我们住的 Utah 在这一点上做得很好，高中有强制的个人理财课。在高中，老师

turns.en: asked a question of who knows what a Roth IRA is and my kids are the only ones in their class that knew what a Roth IRA was, much less had one already that they'd been contributing to for years. There are lots of ways that you can teach your kids personal finance and investing.
turns.zh: 问了个问题：谁知道 Roth IRA 是什么？我的孩子是班上唯一知道 Roth IRA 是什么的，更别说他们已经开了一个、并且往里存了好几年了。有很多方法可以教你的孩子个人理财和投资。

turns.en: Recognize that you have the ability to do that even if you don't know everything, even if you don't consider yourself a hobbyist, it's important to be having these conversations because you don't want them to have the experience you had probably, which is you walked out
turns.zh: 要认识到你有能力这么做，即便你不是什么都懂，即便你不把自己当成一个'爱好者'，进行这些对话也很重要，因为你不会想让他们有你可能有过的那种经历，也就是你在

turns.en: into the world at 18 or 19 or 20 years old knowing nothing and had to learn everything by experience and that's not an awesome way to learn. So sticking with kids, you've often talked about this idea of a 20s fund for your kids can you talk about what that is, what type of account you would recommend for it and
turns.zh: 18、19 或 20 岁时一无所知地走进这个世界，不得不靠亲身经历去学会一切，而那并不是一种很好的学习方式。那么继续聊孩子，你经常谈到这个为孩子设立'20多岁基金'的想法。你能谈谈它是什么、你会推荐用哪种账户、

turns.en: what sorts of investments would go inside it? Sure. The 20s fund idea came out of the fact that I was poor in my 20s. In college, I was literally donating plasma for grocery money, right? I mean, my parents had enough money to fly me home for Christmas and to fly me home
turns.zh: 里面会放什么样的投资吗？好的。'20多岁基金'这个想法，源自我 20 多岁时很穷这个事实。上大学时，我真的是靠献血浆来挣买菜钱，对吧？我是说，我父母有足够的钱让我圣诞飞回家、

turns.en: for the summer and they let me live at home for free while I was doing a summer job during my college years, but that was it. I was on my own for the rest. And so every march or so, I'd run out of money. The money I'd saved up from the summer before and I'd need to get to the end of the school
turns.zh: 暑假飞回家，大学那几年我做暑期工时也让我免费住在家里，但也就这样了。剩下的都得靠我自己。所以每到三月左右，我就把钱花光了——那是我之前一个夏天攒下来的钱——我得撑到学年

turns.en: year without being too hungry and I didn't like that. I missed out on a lot of opportunities in my 20s that I think would have been really cool, like owning a car, like maybe going to Europe, those sorts of things. The first time I ever really went outside the country in a significant way was after
turns.zh: 结束、又不至于太饿，我不喜欢那样。我 20 多岁时错过了很多我觉得本来会很棒的机会，比如拥有一辆车，比如也许去一趟欧洲，那些事。我第一次真正意义地走出国门，是在

turns.en: I graduated from medical school, I was 28 years old. And I just think the 20s are a pretty awesome decade. And if there was ever a time when you could use a little bit more money, even though you don't yet have the capacity to earn it, it's your 20s. And so that's one purpose of the 20s fund is some of my kids don't have that experience.
turns.zh: 我从医学院毕业之后，那时我 28 岁。我就是觉得 20 多岁是很棒的十年。如果说有哪个时候你会需要多一点钱——尽管你还没能力挣到它——那就是你的 20 多岁。所以'20多岁基金'的一个目的，就是让我的一些孩子不必有我那样的经历。

turns.en: So they can do some of those things that you can only do in your 20s and have a little bit more of an enjoyable time than I had. But the other purpose of the 20s fund is that it is a little bit of an early inheritance. Like it's standard to inherit substantially more money than what we give them when they head out the door in their 20s.
turns.zh: 这样他们就能做那些只有 20 多岁才能做的事，过得比我当年更开心一点。但'20多岁基金'的另一个目的，是它有点像是在提前给遗产。按惯例，他们最终继承的钱，会远远多于我们在他们 20 多岁出门闯荡时给他们的那笔。

turns.en: And this lets us see how they manage it. So far, we've been very pleased with what we've seen. But if they ended up being super spend-thrifts, that would tell us when they do get their eventual inheritance, it needs to be in some sort of a spend-thrift trust because they've shown they can't handle a lump sum.
turns.zh: 而这让我们能观察他们如何管理这笔钱。到目前为止，我们对看到的非常满意。但如果他们最后变成超级挥霍者，那就会告诉我们，等他们真正拿到最终遗产时，得放进某种挥霍者信托（spendthrift trust），因为他们已经表明自己没法驾驭一大笔钱。

turns.en: And so I think those are really the two purposes of a 20s fund for us. And you can define this any way you like. Some people would include the Roth IRA. We helped them to do with their earnings as teenagers. Some people would include their 529s for their college savings. But the main fund we're talking about here was a custodial account.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得对我们来说，这才是'20多岁基金'真正的两个目的。你可以按自己喜欢的方式来定义它。有些人会把 Roth IRA 也算进去——我们帮他们用青少年时期的收入去开立。有些人会把用于大学储蓄的 529 计划算进去。但我们这里主要谈的那笔基金，是一个监护账户（custodial account）。

turns.en: This was a UTMA account, which they gained control of at 21. Literally, Vanguard called me up and said, you know, it's time for this to be moved out of your account. So we're moving it over to her account when my child turned 21. And sure enough, the next day, I had no visibility into this account anymore. It was her money. Wow.
turns.zh: 这是一个 UTMA 账户，他们到 21 岁时获得控制权。真的是，Vanguard 打电话给我说，你知道，是时候把这笔钱从你的账户里转出去了，所以等我的孩子满 21 岁时，我们就把它转到她的账户。果然，第二天，我就再也看不到这个账户了。那是她的钱了。哇。

turns.en: And if she wanted to go spend it on whatever she wanted, she could do that. And so that's the account that we use for it is a UTMA account. And so far, children have shown that they're being very, very responsible with that money. And so we're pretty pleased about that. And that's the idea behind a 20s fund.
turns.zh: 如果她想拿去花在任何她想花的东西上，她可以这么做。所以我们用来做这件事的账户就是一个 UTMA 账户。到目前为止，孩子们已经表明他们对这笔钱非常非常负责任。所以我们对此相当满意。这就是'20多岁基金'背后的理念。

turns.en: Is it's just way more useful to inherit money in your 20s than it is the age at which most people inherit money, which is around age 60. By age 60, if you've planned your financial life reasonably well, some big lump sum of money as an inheritance is not going to change your life at all. It's completely useless to you.
turns.zh: 那就是，在 20 多岁继承钱，比在大多数人继承钱的年龄——也就是 60 岁左右——要有用得多。到了 60 岁，如果你把自己的财务人生规划得还算不错，那么作为遗产的一大笔钱根本不会改变你的人生。它对你完全没用。

turns.en: Whereas it could have really made a difference in your life if you had received a decades earlier. Can you talk a little bit more about how the 20s fund has worked in practice for your kids? Do they end up using that money for travel or other things that you sort of had in mind? Yeah.
turns.zh: 而如果早几十年拿到，它本可以真正改变你的人生。你能不能再多谈谈'20多岁基金'在你孩子们身上实际运作得怎么样？他们最后有没有把那笔钱用于旅行，或者你当初设想的其他事情？有。

turns.en: I mean, the idea behind it was travel, a car, a wedding, a honeymoon. Maybe if they need some additional college money, down payment on a house, mission trip, summer in Europe. Those are sort of the ideas behind this 20s fund. And every family is going to be a different size. Some people obviously can't afford to do it at all.
turns.zh: 我是说，它背后的设想就是旅行、一辆车、一场婚礼、一次蜜月。也许如果他们需要一些额外的大学费用、房子的首付、传教之旅、在欧洲过个夏天。这些就是'20多岁基金'背后的那些设想。而每个家庭规模都不一样。有些人显然根本负担不起。

turns.en: You've got to take care of yourself first before you can be giving money to the next generation. But we basically just invested in index funds. I think half of it was in a total stock market index fund. The other half was in a total international stock market index fund, and we made contributions to it.
turns.zh: 你得先照顾好自己，才能给下一代钱。但我们基本上就投了指数基金。我记得一半放在一只全市场股票指数基金里，另一半放在一只全国际市场股票指数基金里，我们往里做了一些投入。

turns.en: Occasionally, they made contributions to it. They received an inheritance from a grandfather of a few thousand dollars. That went into that UTMA account as well. But we've always told them, this is your money. We talked about it being their money. We showed them the statements when they come in, and those quarters, when they lost money,
turns.zh: 偶尔他们也往里投。他们从一位祖父那里继承了几千美元，那也进了那个 UTMA 账户。但我们一直告诉他们，这是你们的钱。我们把它说成是他们的钱。对账单寄来时我们给他们看，那些亏钱的季度，

turns.en: we pointed out that they had lost money. And when the quarters went and done really well, we showed them, look, this is what your money can do. It can make more money than you can make. And so we were able to teach lots of lessons along the way using that fund. But basically, it's now their money, right?
turns.zh: 我们指出来他们亏了钱。而那些表现非常好的季度，我们给他们看：瞧，这就是你的钱能做的事，它赚的钱能比你能赚的还多。所以我们能借这只基金一路上教很多课。但基本上，现在它是他们的钱了，对吧？

turns.en: They can withdraw it and transfer the money to their bank account and pay any capital gains taxes due on it. It's their money that's given to them when they turn 21 in essence. And so far, the only real use we've seen from it is our oldest body used car with it.
turns.zh: 他们可以把它取出来、把钱转到自己的银行账户，并缴纳应付的资本利得税。它本质上是在他们满 21 岁时给他们的钱。到目前为止，我们看到的唯一真正用途，是我们最大的孩子用它买了一辆二手车。

turns.en: The rest of us just been sitting there growing, and I suspect most of them are going to use mostly for a house down payment, giving the housing crisis these days. I'd ask Jim, you've referenced index funds a few times through this conversation. You are part of the Bogleheads community and active contributor to the Bogleheads forum.
turns.zh: 其余的就一直放在那儿增长，我猜他们大多数人会主要用它来付房子首付，鉴于如今的住房危机。我想问问 Jim，你在这场对话里几次提到指数基金。你是 Bogleheads 社群的一员，也是 Bogleheads 论坛的活跃贡献者。

turns.en: You knew Jack Bogle in his lifetime. You attended a celebration of the index funds 50th birthday this past week. Can you talk about your interactions with Jack? Yeah, I was honored to be invited to an opening bell ceremony at the New York Stock Exchange. Fascinating opportunity if you've never been there. It's a beautiful building.
turns.zh: 你在 Jack Bogle 生前就认识他。上周你参加了指数基金 50 岁生日的庆祝活动。你能谈谈你和 Jack 的交往吗？是啊，我很荣幸受邀参加了纽约证券交易所的开市敲钟仪式。如果你从没去过，那是个迷人的机会。那是栋很美的建筑。

turns.en: Feels like it belongs in DC more than New York. It's just that kind of huge columns, high ceilings, kind of a building. But it's interesting to stand on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange. It is not what you've seen in movies that are 20 or 30 years old, where as soon as the
turns.zh: 感觉它更该属于 DC，而不是纽约。就是那种有巨大圆柱、挑高天花板的建筑。但站在纽约证券交易所的大厅里很有意思。它并不是你在二三十年前的电影里看到的那样——铃一响，

turns.en: bell rings, everybody starts screaming and holding papers in their hand. There's a big mosh pit in the middle, right? It's all electronic now. It's actually not even that loud. And standing right behind you are the folks from CNBC, given their daily market commentary in a little booth.
turns.zh: 所有人就开始尖叫、手里挥舞着纸单，中间有一大群人挤成一团（mosh pit），对吧？现在全都是电子化的了。其实甚至没那么吵。而就在你身后站着的是 CNBC 的人，在一个小隔间里做他们每天的行情点评。

turns.en: And it's still pretty interesting to recognize that that is where, in large part, it's kind of the mecca of capitalism. And so it was a wonderful opportunity to be there with staff from Vanguard, as well as a whole bunch of people who have helped get the word out about index funds and index investing over the last 20 and 30 and 40 years.
turns.zh: 认识到那里在很大程度上就是资本主义的圣地，仍然挺有意思的。所以能在那里、和 Vanguard 的员工、以及一大批在过去二三四十年里帮助把指数基金和指数投资推广出去的人在一起，是个很棒的机会。

turns.en: And so it was a real who's who of the indexing community that was invited to that ceremony and a brunch reception following. There's a great opportunity to be there. I only actually met Jack Bogel one time in person, and it was at a Bogel's conference. I think it was in, oh, it must have been 2016 or 17 or something like that.
turns.zh: 所以受邀参加那场仪式、以及随后的早午餐招待会的，是指数化社群里名副其实的'名人堂'阵容，是个在场的好机会。其实我只当面见过 Jack Bogle 一次，那是在一次 Bogleheads 会议上。我记得那是——哦，应该是 2016 或 17 年前后吧。

turns.en: I was hoping to meet him earlier, probably 2008, but he had to miss the conference due to being in the hospital with his heart. Those may not know this, but he had a heart transplant and lived for many years after getting that heart transplant. And so he had to deal with substantial medical issues in the last couple of decades of his
turns.zh: 我本来希望更早见到他，大概是 2008 年，但他因为心脏问题住院，不得不缺席那次会议。有些人可能不知道，他做过心脏移植，并在移植后又活了很多年。所以在他生命的

turns.en: life. But one of the most remarkable things about Jack Bogel is that had he run Vanguard like Fidelity was run or some of these other big investing firms, he would have been a billionaire. And he died wealthy, right? He was able to endow hundreds and hundreds of scholarships at the private high school he had attended.
turns.zh: 最后二十年里，他不得不应对重大的健康问题。但关于 Jack Bogle 最了不起的一点是，如果他像 Fidelity 那样、或像其他一些大型投资公司那样去经营 Vanguard，他本可以成为一个亿万富翁。他去世时很富有，对吧？他得以在他读过的那所私立高中设立数百份奖学金。

turns.en: And do a whole bunch of other wonderful things, but he did not die of billionaire. And the reason why is because he essentially gave his firm away to the investors. And it was a really remarkable thing. And once he did that, he took that mindset with him and his sheer force of will with him
turns.zh: 还做了很多其他很棒的事，但他去世时并不是亿万富翁。原因就在于，他本质上把自己的公司送给了投资者。这是件非常了不起的事。而一旦他这么做了，他就带着那种心态、带着他那纯粹的意志力，

turns.en: throughout the next four or five decades of his life. And really tried to do the right thing for people. And when he'd stand up and make a fuss about some change that had happened in the financial services industry, you could be sure that he really did feel that way.
turns.zh: 走过了他接下来四五十年的人生。他真的努力去为人们做正确的事。当他站起来、为金融服务行业里发生的某个变化大声疾呼时，你可以确信他真的就是这么想的。

turns.en: And he felt like if it, you know, this new innovation or whatever, you know, a classic example might be he was very against ETFs. He was worried people would just start day trading them. And obviously there's lots of people that do day trade ETFs, but you knew where he was coming from. And he really did care about the individual investor.
turns.zh: 他觉得，如果这个新创新之类的——你知道，一个经典的例子是他非常反对 ETF。他担心人们会开始日内交易（day trade）它们。显然确实有很多人日内交易 ETF，但你明白他是从哪里出发的。他是真的关心个人投资者。

turns.en: And that's what I appreciated the most about Jack Bogel is it was a refreshing mindset shift compared to most of the people in the financial services industry. In addition to your work on the white code investor, you're still a practicing physician. How does your work in the ER contribute to and help inform the other work that you do

turns.zh: 对很多人来说，那是个压力非常大的地方，也是个非常不愉快的地方。但能在他们人生的那个时刻陪在他们身边，是一种真正的荣幸。不过就投资而言，我觉得你能从急诊室里得到的最有力的一课，是人生中有些东西比钱更重要。

turns.zh: 其中之一是你的健康，其中之一是你的家人。要记住这一点，并始终把钱放在你人生中应有的位置上——它是一个工具，帮助你建立快乐、建立生产力、建立目标和善意，并帮助他人。
